prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable frequency standards at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock (B049), Katori and Ye, and I have not changed my configuration since round 1. What persuades me is that the idea is a simple, general mechanism: at the magic wavelength the trap light shifts both clock levels equally, so thousands of neutral atoms can be held Doppler- and recoil-free without perturbing the line. That trades the single-ion limit on atom number against the ensemble limit on systematics, which neither the comb (2005) nor the control of single ions (2012) addressed. The systematics (blackbody, polarizability, collisional and density shifts) are understood quantitatively, the result is reproduced at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and cross-continent comparisons show that the stability is real rather than a single-laboratory number. Because the citation names the mechanism and its realization, it also answers the chair's question about discovery versus instrument: the new thing is a regime of many-atom interrogation, not a better number. I do not think the prize needs a measured departure from known physics to be a discovery-class result; the clock is already the tool that tests constants and relativistic redshift at the millimetre scale. I accept Ye's name because the realization at 10^-18 and the demonstration that many-body and density effects can be controlled are what made the idea a working clock rather than a proposal.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is the one Olsson and Lindroth press: Katori holds the proposal and first realization, and Ye's contribution is arguably a superb second wave of execution, so the two-name credit may overstate Ye's share of the original idea. The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is also real and must be handled explicitly in the citation, and Lemonde, Gill, Takamoto, Lisdat, Ludlow and others sit outside the two names. Finally, the clocks have not yet delivered a surprising physical result, so a committee that wants measured departures from known theory would find the case early; the pending redefinition of the second is not a precondition for me but would help.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether the prize would still stand if only Katori were credited, since Ye's role may be a better-executed second wave rather than the original invention and realization.
responses.response: It would stand, and that is what fixes the priority: the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration are Katori's. But I would keep Ye. The mechanism only becomes a clock when the many-atom systematics, including the density-dependent and many-body shifts one might have feared would spoil the scheme, are shown to be controllable at 10^-18. That is part of the realization, not a lifetime award. I therefore support your own suggested safeguard, that the citation name the invention and its realization, so that the two names are tied to specific work and not to general precision-measurement careers or to Ye's molecule programme. If the committee prefers a strict priority reading, Katori alone is a defensible fallback, but I think the two-name version is more accurate.

responses.point: Lindroth asks which measurement convinced me about stochastic thermodynamics (B045), and says she cannot judge whether its experimental validation is decisive enough.
responses.response: The convincing tests are the single-molecule pulling experiments, in which Jarzynski and Crooks relations recover equilibrium free energies from nonequilibrium work distributions, plus later colloidal and electronic-circuit realizations. They are real, but they test an exact identity that follows from the dynamics, and the measurement does not discover a surprise. Together with the credit problem (four names plus Gallavotti, Cohen and the experimentalists), that is why I no longer lead with it and have dropped it from my alternatives. Your point that the clock is strongest on maturity and on every shift being understood in quantitative detail is the criterion I find decisive, and it is why B049 now clearly outranks B045 for me.

responses.point: Pearce proposes a two-part prize adding B047 (IceCube, Halzen alone) to B049, while conceding the single-name credit is weak and that he would drop it if the committee cannot document Halzen's decisive role.
responses.response: I appreciate the candour, and I accept that neutrino astronomy is a genuine new window and that the diffuse flux is secure. But I cannot support B047 as a second part on the supplied credit: one name for a cubic-kilometre collaboration, with AMANDA lineage you cannot separate, is a correction waiting to happen, and the source identifications (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) are statistically more modest than the diffuse flux. I would rather the committee give the clock a clean single-part prize than carry a second part that its proponent says may need dropping. If a second part is wanted, I would prefer it to be one with a clear three-name credit (B048 or B024), though I regard neither as settled.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B024 first and says the clock is plausible but not urgent, treating the theta-13 measurement as a discovery from nature with wide confirmation.
responses.response: I take the discovery argument seriously, and I have moved B024 into my alternatives for that reason. Our rule, however, is to be sure we name the people who did the original work, and I cannot show from the supplied material that Luk, Kim and Wang are uncontroversial given the near-simultaneous Daya Bay, RENO and Double Chooz results, and the 2015 oscillation prize makes distinctness harder to argue. I also disagree that not urgent counts against the clock: urgency is not our criterion, and maturity, as the cross-continent clock comparisons show, is already excellent.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B048 (Kane, Mele, Molenkamp) as a single-part prize, arguing that topological insulators are a new state of matter with a decisive theory-plus-experiment pairing.
responses.response: I find the physics persuasive and keep B048 as my first alternative. I do not think the 2016 topological prize is fatal, since the Z2 invariant and the quantum spin Hall effect are a distinct step from the Chern-insulator and Kosterlitz-Thouless physics honoured there. My reservation is the same one you and others raise: omitting Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed HgTe, and the three-dimensional work of Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Hasan, means the committee would be choosing among several plausible laureate sets. If you can show that the Molenkamp edge-conductance quantisation has been reproduced beyond his group, I would weigh B048 more heavily.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which depends on whether the citation can name the magic-wavelength many-atom regime precisely.

Whether Ye's share is part of the invention and realization or a later performance step, and whether Katori alone is the more defensible attribution; I have not checked priority against primary papers.
Whether a measured departure (constants drift, geodesy at scale, dark-matter couplings) is required for a discovery-class result, or whether the new regime itself suffices.
Whether B048 or B024 is the better fallback; my fit to condensed matter and neutrino physics is as a neighbour, not a specialist.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I work in the same Gothenburg physics environment as Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson (Chalmers), with no specific collaboration recorded; none of the candidates I name is from that environment, and I do not request recusal on any shortlisted candidate. I have no tie to Katori, Ye or their groups.
